def: How strongly a volume of rain echoes the radar pulse: the sum of the sixth powers of the drop diameters, in mm⁶ m⁻³. Dominated by the biggest drops.
Reflectivity on a decibel scale, 10·log₁₀(Z). Drizzle is around 15–25 dBZ, heavy convection 45–55.
Depth of water reaching the ground per hour, in mm h⁻¹: drop volume times fall speed, summed. Weighted by roughly D³·⁷, not D⁶.
A fixed power law Z = aR^b used to turn reflectivity into rain rate. It only holds for one drop size distribution, which is the ambiguity the book is about.
How many drops of each size are in a cubic metre, N(D). DPR models it as a normalised gamma distribution with parameters Dₘ, N_w and μ.
Mass-weighted mean drop diameter, in mm: the typical size of the drops carrying the water. One of the two DSD numbers DPR retrieves.
Normalised intercept of the gamma DSD — how many drops there are, independent of their size. Usually quoted as log₁₀ N_w.
Shape parameter of the gamma DSD. DPR assumes it (μ = 3) rather than retrieving it.
DPR's 13.6 GHz channel (wavelength 2.2 cm). Attenuated relatively little by rain; drawn in amber throughout.
DPR's 35.5 GHz channel (wavelength 8.4 mm). More sensitive to light rain and snow, but attenuated heavily; drawn in teal throughout.
A passive instrument that measures microwave brightness from the whole column at once. It cannot tell at what height the rain is.
The GPM Microwave Imager, the radiometer flying with DPR on the Core Observatory, with a 904 km swath.
An orbit that crosses each latitude at the same local times every day. GPM deliberately avoids it so it samples the whole daily cycle of rain.
The strip of ground the radar scans as it flies: about 245 km wide for DPR, in 49 beams across track.
Straight down beneath the satellite. Beams away from nadir look at the ground at an angle, up to 17°.
One slice of the echo along the beam, 125 m long in the standard product. A ray is a column of range bins.
The lowest range bin not contaminated by the ground echo. Below it the radar is blind; it rises off nadir.
The highest range bin with a detectable echo.
Loss of radar signal as the pulse passes through rain, out and back. It makes the measured reflectivity weaker the deeper the beam goes.
Path-integrated attenuation: the total two-way loss down to a given bin, in dB.
The classic analytic attenuation correction. Its denominator shrinks as attenuation builds, so in heavy rain small errors blow up.
Estimates PIA by comparing the ground echo inside rain with its rain-free value nearby.
Dual-frequency ratio: Ku reflectivity minus Ka reflectivity, in dB. Independent of N_w, so it measures drop size.
Scattering by drops much smaller than the wavelength: backscatter grows as D⁶. True for Ku in light rain.
Exact scattering by a sphere of any size. When drops approach the wavelength, backscatter falls below the Rayleigh D⁶ law — first at Ka.
Widespread, steady rain from a melting snow layer, usually with a bright band.
Rain from vigorous updraughts: tall, intense and patchy, without a bright band.
The height of the 0 °C isotherm, where falling snow starts to melt.
A thin layer of enhanced echo just below the freezing level, where melting snowflakes are wet but still large.
The layer below the freezing level where particles are part ice, part water.
The Solver's adjustment factor on the R–Dₘ relation, swept from 0.2 to 5 to reconcile the observations with the prior.
One file of Level-2 data: a single orbit's worth of swath.
Attenuation-corrected reflectivity in the Level-2 product.
Retrieved precipitation rate, mm h⁻¹, per range bin (or near the surface).
The retrieved DSD parameters, N_w and Dₘ, per range bin.
Rain type flag: stratiform, convective or other.
Bright-band detection flag.
